question: How do the PRD v2 changes routed to simple-login.web (H16: the time zone and my bookings with Cancel on Home, the Rooms screen with its date and booking form, every time in the user's zone per ADR-002, D4 revisited, stubs from booking-api@v1 and the touched profile-api@v2 fixtures) split into appended phases?

options.label: five phases: client and rig (5); time functions (6); Home (7); Rooms and navigation (8); booking form (9)
options.consequence: Follows interfaces-first: 5 is the typed boundary (booking-api@v1 client, timeZone in the profile, the fixture stub, the ambient zone), 6 the pure time core, 7 to 9 the screens with the App wiring each needs. 5 and 6 run in parallel; 7, 8 and 9 serialise on App.tsx and the Rooms screen. Each estimated at 340 to 400 lines and at most 7 tasks.

options.label: six phases: the same, with the App wiring and navigation in a last composition phase
options.consequence: Screens 7 and 8 could run in parallel and the last phase is pure composition, but Home and Rooms then cannot be reached in the running app until that phase, every screen still needs App changes to compile once its props change, and one frontend developer (PRD v2 Team and delivery) gains nothing from a second lane.

options.label: four phases: Rooms list and booking form together
options.consequence: One fewer cycle, but the merged Rooms phase comes to about 760 lines and over 10 tasks: over one review sitting.

chosen: five phases: client and rig (5); time functions (6); Home (7); Rooms and navigation (8); booking form (9)
why: hsdd/conventions.md names interfaces-first: types and the contract-bounded client first, pure logic next, effects and composition behind them. The client with its every-fixture tests and the stub changes is about 400 lines on its own; the time functions with their clock-change tests about 340; Home with Cancel about 385; Rooms with navigation about 400; the form about 360, each within one Phase Equivalent. Composition is spread over the screen phases as web.3 did (it composed the app with the Home screen), so every phase leaves the app runnable. If the web lane had two developers, the six-phase split would have led for its parallel screen lane.
evidence: PRD v2 US-2, US-4, US-5, US-6, Screens

question: Q-060: how does the web app implement ADR-002's conversions on Node.js 24, which has no global Temporal: Intl alone, a library built on Intl, or a Temporal polyfill?

options.label: Intl alone, in one module of pure functions
options.consequence: No new package; every function takes the zone as an argument and reads wall dates and times through Intl.DateTimeFormat formatToParts. The start of a date is found by scanning quarter-hour instants, so no offset or clock-change date is hand-coded. The module is small and every rule is visible in it.

options.label: a library built on Intl (for example date-fns-tz)
options.consequence: Ready-made zoned conversions, but a new dependency for about 140 lines of code, and the repeated-hour mark and the date marks of ADR-002 Decision 7 still have to be written by hand on top of it.

options.label: a Temporal polyfill
options.consequence: The API ADR-002's model maps to most directly, but a large dependency in the browser bundle and a second time-zone database beside the runtime's Intl data that ADR-002 Decision 4 names.

chosen: Intl alone, in one module of pure functions
why: ADR-002 Decision 4 says the conversions use the runtime's Intl time-zone data and no node hand-codes an offset. The experiment prototyped every function the plan needs with Intl alone under TZ=Asia/Kolkata and reproduced the three rooms fixtures' query paths, London's 23- and 25-hour days, 92 and 100 quarter hours, the BST and GMT marks and PRD v2's example strings. A need for zone arithmetic beyond one date and its quarter hours (recurring bookings, say) would have made a library worth its weight.

question: Q-062: profile-api@v2 G5 says a profile without timeZone comes from a backend that predates the field and the consumer then shows no time. Today a 200 profile missing a field is 'unavailable', which would hide all of Home. How does the web app treat a profile without a usable time zone?

options.label: timeZone optional: the profile still decodes; Home shows its other rows and no booking time
options.consequence: Profile gains timeZone as the name received or null when absent; a non-string is a malformed 200 as before. Home shows the Time zone row as 'Not available', and in place of My bookings and Book a room one line, 'Bookings need your time zone, which is not available.', with no booking request. A name Intl refuses counts as absent, so no format call can throw.

options.label: timeZone required like phone: a profile without it is 'unavailable'
options.consequence: One rule for every field, but a web app shipped before the backend's time-zone phase would answer every sign-in with the network message and show no Home at all.

chosen: timeZone optional: the profile still decodes; Home shows its other rows and no booking time
why: The backend and the web app ship separately (PRD v2 Team and delivery), and profile-api@v2's Versioning says a consumer can meet a profile without timeZone until the producer's phase ships; G5 asks for no time rather than a guess, not for no profile. Keeping sign-in and the profile working while only times are withheld is the narrowest reading of G5. The experiment showed Intl accepts '+07:00' and refuses 'Mars/Olympus', so the Intl check guards against a crash only. Had the producer and consumer been required to ship together, requiring the field would have been simpler.

question: Q-058, Q-063: D1 notices expiry only when GET /api/me answers 401 on load, and cites profile-api@v1. booking-api@v1 G16 answers 401 UNAUTHORIZED at every endpoint, so a list, a Cancel or a Book can be the first request to meet an expired token (PRD v2 AC-2.3). How is D1 revisited?

options.label: any request carrying the token that answers 401 ends the session; D1 amended in place with a dated marker
options.consequence: GET /api/me on load and every booking-api@v1 call (Home's list and Cancel, Rooms' list and Book) clear the session and show Login with the AC-2.3 message; still no timer. D1 cites profile-api@v2 G7 and booking-api@v1 G16 instead of profile-api@v1, and keeps a marker naming what it said before.

options.label: keep D1 as written; a booking call's 401 shows an inline message
options.consequence: The user stays on a screen whose every action fails, with a message that does not match AC-2.3's, until the next reload.

options.label: a new decision superseding D1, D1 left as it was
options.consequence: The decisions list would hold a stale rule beside its replacement, and every phase context that cites D1 would carry the old one.

chosen: any request carrying the token that answers 401 ends the session; D1 amended in place with a dated marker
why: AC-2.3 asks that an expired session sends the user to Login with its message, wherever it is noticed; booking-api@v1 G16 and profile-api@v2 G7 make the 401 the same body and indistinguishable from an unknown token, so one handling fits all. The file's own convention amends decisions in place with a dated marker (D3, D5). profile-api@v1 stays stable, but D1's sentence is about the v2 endpoint the node now uses (Q-058). An ADR or contract that let the web app tell expiry from an unknown token would have changed the message per case.

question: Q-063, DEC-012: D4 says 'No router (RFC §6): the screen is a function of the session value'. With three screens, how does the app move between them, which screen shows after sign-in and on reload, and does Rooms keep a URL?

options.label: no router and no URL: the signed-in screen is held in memory; sign-in and reload show Home
options.consequence: The flow's signed-in state gains which screen shows, Home or Rooms; Book a room and Rooms' Home button switch it; only the session is stored (D2), so a reload on Rooms shows Home, and Rooms opens on today each time it shows. RFC-001 §6's choice holds with three screens; no package is added.

options.label: a hash per screen (#/rooms) read on load
options.consequence: A reload keeps the user on Rooms and the back button works, but the app gains URL parsing and a second source of truth beside the session, which RFC-001 §6 ruled out ('There are no URLs per screen').

options.label: a router package
options.consequence: Deep links and history for free, but a dependency and a structure RFC-001 §6 set aside, for one extra screen nothing links into.

chosen: no router and no URL: the signed-in screen is held in memory; sign-in and reload show Home
why: RFC-001 §6 (normative) made the app a function of state with no URLs per screen; PRD v2 Screens draws Home with Book a room and Rooms with a Home button and nothing that links into Rooms from outside. A reload showing Home costs one click, and PRD v2 AC-2.2 asks only that a reload keeps the user signed in. The RFC's two-screen premise is flagged upstream by the intake record (DEC-013). A PRD criterion to share or bookmark a Rooms date would have made the hash lead.

question: Q-061: the fixture stub matches String(input) against request.path, but the rooms fixtures' paths carry unencoded colons while URLSearchParams writes %3A. Does the client send the instants unencoded, or does the stub compare decoded URLs?

options.label: the client writes the instants unencoded; the stub keeps its exact match
options.consequence: The query is built as /api/rooms?from={from}&to={to} from toISOString() strings, whose characters are all legal in a query; the recorded call equals the fixture's path, so a test proves the exact request. booking-api@v1 accepts both forms.

options.label: the client uses URLSearchParams; the stub decodes both sides before comparing
options.consequence: The client uses the platform encoder, but the stub then accepts requests the fixtures do not name byte for byte, and every recorded path differs from its fixture's.

chosen: the client writes the instants unencoded; the stub keeps its exact match
why: The values are instants the client produced itself with toISOString() (digits, '-', ':', '.', 'T', 'Z'), so encoding adds nothing; booking-api@v1's GET /api/rooms section says the producer decodes either form. Keeping the stub exact keeps every web test a proof of the exact request the fixture names. A query value that could hold user text would have made the encoder lead.
evidence: booking-api@v1 Validation (consumers match on method and path)

question: Home lists my bookings that have not ended (booking-api@v1 G14), which includes one in progress that can no longer be cancelled (AC-6.2). Is Cancel shown on every listed booking, or hidden by the browser's clock once a booking has started?

options.label: Cancel on every listed booking; the backend's answer decides
options.consequence: A Cancel on a started booking gets 422 BOOKING_STARTED and the message 'That booking has already started, so it cannot be cancelled.', then the list is fetched again. The browser's clock decides nothing on Home.

options.label: hide Cancel when the browser's clock reads the start or later
options.consequence: No button that always fails, but the browser's clock then decides what the user may do, which ADR-002 Decision 5 does not list (it names only the Rooms screen's opening date and leaving past times out of the form), and a drifting laptop clock hides or shows the button wrongly near a start.

chosen: Cancel on every listed booking; the backend's answer decides
why: ADR-002 Decision 5 and booking-api@v1 G7 say the backend's clock decides and the browser's clock decides nothing, and the ADR names the only two uses it allows. The cost is one refused Cancel per in-progress booking, which the message explains. An ADR-002 sentence allowing the browser's clock to hide Cancel on a started booking would have flipped this.

question: PRD v2 fixes only AC-5.3's overlap message among the booking answers. What does the web app show for each other booking-api@v1 answer, given G18 (branch on error.code, never show error.message)?

options.label: one message per code in the web's own copy table, worded like the contract's messages where they read well
options.consequence: BOOKING_STARTED on Book 'That time has already started.', BOOKING_TOO_LONG 'A booking can last at most 8 hours.', BOOKING_TOO_FAR_AHEAD 'A booking can start at most 365 days ahead.', VALIDATION_FAILED on Book 'That booking is not valid. Check the times and the title.', a 201 'Booked.'; on Cancel, BOOKING_STARTED 'That booking has already started, so it cannot be cancelled.', BOOKING_NOT_FOUND 'That booking was already cancelled.', BOOKING_NOT_YOURS 'You can cancel only your own bookings.'; an empty list '(no bookings)'; 401 is D1 and anything unexpected D3's network message. The strings live in messages.ts, keyed by the client's reasons, so a backend wording change moves nothing.

options.label: show error.message as received
options.consequence: No copy to maintain, but G18 forbids it, the backend's wording becomes UI copy, and AC-5.3's sentence could not be written that way at all.

options.label: one generic failure message for every refusal
options.consequence: Least copy, but the user cannot tell a time that has started from a booking that is too long, and PRD v2's Goal (a free room in under a minute) suffers.

chosen: one message per code in the web's own copy table, worded like the contract's messages where they read well
why: D3 already set 'one message per failure' for sign-in; this extends it to the booking answers. booking-api@v1 G18 requires branching on the code; the contract's messages are plain and correct, so reusing their wording costs nothing and keeps the screens and the API consistent, while the web owns the strings. '(no bookings)' is PRD v2 Screens' own copy. Product copy for these cases in the PRD would have replaced the table.
evidence: PRD v2 AC-5.3, AC-6.2, AC-6.3, Screens

question: Q-061: the booking form may offer end times up to start + 8 hours and dates up to 365 days ahead, but the backend's answer decides; ADR-002 Decision 4 gives the form the picked date's quarter-hour instants and Decision 5 lets the browser's clock leave past times out. Which start and end times, and which dates, does the form offer?

options.label: starts after the browser's clock; ends up to start + 8 hours or the next date's start; any date
options.consequence: Starts: the picked date's quarter-hour instants later than the browser's clock. Ends: the quarter-hour instants after the start, up to whichever comes first, start + 8 hours of elapsed time (G9) or the start of the next date (labelled 'Fri 6 Nov 00:00'). The date input is not capped: a date past 365 days gets BOOKING_TOO_FAR_AHEAD from the backend, and past dates still show their bookings. A date with no start left says 'No times left on this date.'

options.label: every quarter-hour instant of the date for both, with no clock and no length filter
options.consequence: Simplest, but most of today's offers are refused as started, and ends past 8 hours are refused as too long.

options.label: also cap the date input at today + 365 days
options.consequence: Fewer refusals, but the Rooms list then cannot show far dates either, and the web would restate the backend's limit in a second place.

chosen: starts after the browser's clock; ends up to start + 8 hours or the next date's start; any date
why: ADR-002 Decision 4 confines the form to the picked date's instants and Decision 5 allows leaving past times out; offering only ends within G9 avoids a refusal the form can foresee without deciding anything (the backend still answers). The date input stays free because the same date drives the read-only rooms list (AC-4.2) and the backend decides how far ahead (G10). The experiment shows every 201 POST fixture's start and end are among the offers with the browser clock at the fixture's clock; book-started's start is not, so its test sets an earlier clock, as ADR-002 Consequences describe. A PRD rule allowing bookings across midnight would have extended the ends past the next date's start.

question: booking-api@v1's fixtures hold no my-bookings list containing a booking that a cancel fixture cancels (cancel-my-booking cancels ayu's ...031, which no list fixture names; my-bookings-budi lists ...011, ...013, ...015, ...016). How do Home's tests press Cancel on a listed booking against fixtures?

options.label: answer the DELETE of the listed booking with a cancel fixture's response unchanged, at that booking's path
options.consequence: A stub helper serves a fixture's response for a path the test names; the status and body are the fixture's byte for byte, only the id in the request path is the listed booking's. The client's own tests (web.5) send each cancel fixture at its own path, so each exact request is still proven once. No contract change.

options.label: request booking-api@v1 to add a my-bookings fixture holding a cancellable id
options.consequence: A pure fixture walk, but the answer would change what simple-login.backend's unshipped phases replay (35 fixtures become 36), which the intake record's insert rule turns into a phase-plan-append and a reconcile on the backend, for a test convenience.

options.label: inject client results into Home instead of stubbing fetch
options.consequence: No fixture needed, but Home's tests would no longer go through the client and the fixtures, against the node's Isolation strategy.

chosen: answer the DELETE of the listed booking with a cancel fixture's response unchanged, at that booking's path
why: hsdd-phase-plan says consuming phases test against the fixtures, never hand-rolled mocks; the response a test sees stays the fixture's, and only the request path, which the stub uses to choose an answer, carries the listed id. web.4's App tests already derive a fixture variant the same way (a 200 without phone). The request option's cost is a rewrite of two backend phases under the insert rule. Had booking-api@v1 still been unplanned on the producer side, the request would have led.

question: Tier choice: the time functions (simple-login.web.6) are pure, which the skill's default puts at spot-check, but they carry AC-4.4 and every display rule of ADR-002 Decision 7. Which review tier?

options.label: full-review
options.consequence: The full artifact set and a reviewer who reads the diff and the clock-change tests; costs a longer sitting for about 340 lines.

options.label: spot-check
options.consequence: A glance at the diff and the gate; the tests pin the outcomes, but a wrong expected value in a test passes a glance just as a wrong function does.

why: ADR-002 Consequences make the web app's isolated tests on both change days the place London's clock changes are proven for this node, and the repeated-hour and date marks are easy to get subtly wrong (an off-by-one at a day's start, a mark on the wrong end). The skill's tier table puts business logic at full-review; these functions are the node's business logic for time. Had the integration node's browser tests been the only proof wanted, spot-check would have been enough.

question: Q-063, Isolation strategy: every web test runs with TZ set to a zone that is neither account's nor UTC (ADR-002 Consequences). Where is it set, and how is it proven?

options.label: TZ=Asia/Kolkata in the web's test and gate scripts, with a guard test
options.consequence: 'gate' becomes 'tsc --noEmit && TZ=Asia/Kolkata vitest run && vite build' and 'test' 'TZ=Asia/Kolkata vitest run'; a test fails unless the ambient zone resolves to Asia/Calcutta or Asia/Kolkata, so a run that loses the variable fails instead of passing on a laptop set to Jakarta or London. The root's npm test calls the web gate unchanged.

options.label: set process.env.TZ in vite.config.ts's test section
options.consequence: Works from any entry point, but depends on the runtime applying a TZ change made after start-up in every Vitest worker, which nothing in the repository has checked.

chosen: TZ=Asia/Kolkata in the web's test and gate scripts, with a guard test
why: A variable set before the process starts is inherited by every worker; the experiments ran Node with TZ=Asia/Kolkata and saw the ambient zone reported as Asia/Calcutta and 02:00Z read as 07 hours. The guard test makes the setting checked rather than assumed, whichever way Vitest is started. Asia/Kolkata is ADR-002's own example. A contributor on Windows, where the inline assignment fails, would have made the config route lead.

question: ADR-002 Decision 7: 'A time whose date, in the zone it is shown in, is not the date its line is about carries its own date.' On Rooms, the room's local times sit in the line of the picked date, so a London booking from 16:30 to 17:30 on 4 November shown to a Jakarta user on 5 November reads '(Wed 4 Nov 16:30 to Wed 4 Nov 17:30 in London)'. Is the rule applied literally, or does an end carry its date only when it differs from its start's?

options.label: literally: each time against the line's date (the picked date on Rooms and in the overlap message, the start's date on Home)
options.consequence: Matches the ADR's sentence and its example ('23:00 to Fri 6 Nov 02:00'); the integration node, which reads the ADR and not this plan, asserts the same strings. Some room-local lines repeat a date.

options.label: an end carries its date only when it differs from its start's
options.consequence: Shorter lines ('(Wed 4 Nov 16:30 to 17:30 in London)'), but a reading the ADR does not state, which the integration node's browser tests could assert differently.

chosen: literally: each time against the line's date (the picked date on Rooms and in the overlap message, the start's date on Home)
why: The ADR states one rule per time and DEC-032 put it in the ADR so the integration node asserts the same strings; a web-only refinement would split the two. The experiment gives the exact strings for the three rooms fixtures, including the repeated date on Kew's Handover line. An ADR-002 amendment shortening the room-local form would change it; it is flagged in the report for the owner.

question: Q-059: the header's Sources entry for hsdd/context/prd-simple-login.v2.md lists (US-1, US-2, US-3, Screens, Scope). Which PRD v2 sections join it for the appended phases, and in what order?

options.label: add US-4, US-5, US-6, Demo accounts, Rooms, Team and delivery, in PRD v2's order
options.consequence: The entry reads (US-1, US-2, US-3, US-4, US-5, US-6, Screens, Demo accounts, Rooms, Scope, Team and delivery): every section a new phase or decision cites. No section is removed. hsdd-reconcile's version ripple (H17) copies it into the root's embedded summary.

options.label: add only US-4, US-5 and US-6
options.consequence: The stories the Overview already cites, but the Home rows' time zones (Demo accounts), the rooms with their offices (Rooms) and the reason a profile may lack timeZone (Team and delivery) would be cited by phases yet missing from Sources.

options.label: append the new sections after the existing ones
options.consequence: Keeps the old list's order untouched, but the entry reads out of the PRD's order (Scope before US-4).

chosen: add US-4, US-5, US-6, Demo accounts, Rooms, Team and delivery, in PRD v2's order
why: hsdd-phase-plan's Change Requests rule: the request's path joins Sources with the sections that govern this node, appended and never replacing an entry; the path is already there (S14, DEC-122), so the sections join it. US-4 to US-6 govern web.7 to web.9; Demo accounts gives Home's time zone values (web.7); Rooms gives the four rooms with offices and seats (web.8); Team and delivery is why a profile can lack timeZone (D7). Goal, Constraints and Success are the backend's and the integration node's. Every existing section stays; only their neighbours change.
evidence: PRD v2 US-4, US-5, US-6, Demo accounts, Rooms, Team and delivery

question: Q-064: the Overview's 'three screens (PRD v2 Screens)' cites a section that draws only Home and Rooms; cite (PRD v2 US-1, Screens). Does this phase-plan-append change the Overview?

options.label: leave the Overview; route the citation to the run for the segment's align
options.consequence: Append mode writes summary rows, phase sections, graph nodes, a pending block, Sources entries and the plan's own decisions; the Overview is hsdd-spec's text. The align that follows the handoffs makes citation changes, so the fix lands there or in a later spec touch.

options.label: change the citation here
options.consequence: Closes the item at once with a one-token edit inside the write set, but a phase-plan step would edit hsdd-spec's prose, which append mode's list of what it writes does not include.

chosen: leave the Overview; route the citation to the run for the segment's align
why: hsdd-phase-plan's Append Mode names what it appends, and the Overview is not among them; DEC-128 found the sentence wrong only in its citation, so nothing in the plan depends on it. hsdd-reconcile's align makes citation changes only, which is exactly this. Had no align been scheduled in the segment, the small edit here would have led.

question: The appended phases collide on files (web.7 and web.8 on App.tsx, session/flow.ts and HomeScreen.tsx; web.8 and web.9 on the Rooms screen), and the summary table has no Collides with column. Does the table gain the column, which adds a cell to the four shipped rows?

options.label: add the column; shipped rows read 'none'
options.consequence: The table states every collision the phase sections state, as the skill's template does when any phase collides; the shipped rows keep every value they had and gain one empty-list cell.

options.label: keep the table's columns; collisions only in the phase sections
options.consequence: No shipped row changes at all, but the human index no longer shows which phases serialise, and the table and the sections differ in what they list.

chosen: add the column; shipped rows read 'none'
why: hsdd-phase-plan omits the column only when no phase collides, and its checklist asks that the table match the phase sections. Append mode keeps shipped rows as a ledger; a 'none' cell for a column they never had changes none of their values. The template's dash for an empty cell is replaced by 'none', per the skill's rendering rule and the run's prose rules. Had the skill said shipped rows are byte-frozen, the sections-only option would have led.

question: Which of this node's phases do the confirm entries name as consumers of booking-api@v1 (provisionally [simple-login.web.5], DEC-053), profile-api@v2 and auth-api@v1?

options.label: every phase whose tests read the contract's fixtures
options.consequence: booking-api@v1: web.5, web.7, web.8, web.9. profile-api@v2: web.4 (shipped), web.5, web.7, web.8. auth-api@v1: web.1 to web.4 (shipped), web.8, whose App walk signs in through login-success. web.6 reads no fixture and consumes nothing. The same rule auth-api@v1's 2026-10-31 Versioning applied when it added web.3 and web.4 for their App tests.

options.label: only the phase that builds each client function
options.consequence: booking-api@v1 would name web.5 alone, but web.7 to web.9 stub fetch with its fixtures and break when they change, and a checkpoint would not see them as consumers.

chosen: every phase whose tests read the contract's fixtures
why: A consumer is a phase that breaks when the contract or its fixtures change; auth-api@v1's own Versioning (2026-10-31) counted web.3 and web.4 for reading login-success in App tests, and the precedent in simple-login.backend's append kept a shipped phase in its confirm list. Listing shipped phases keeps reconcile from dropping them. Had consumers been defined as phases calling the endpoint in production code only, the narrower list would have led.

question: Does the booking-api@v1 client check that each instant it receives is in the toISOString() form, or pass the strings through to the time functions?

options.label: check: an instant not equal to its own toISOString() makes the answer 'unavailable'
options.consequence: One line per decoder; a string without 'Z' never reaches Date.parse, which would read it in the ambient zone, the exact failure ADR-002 guards against. A producer bug shows the network message instead of a wrong time.

options.label: pass the strings through
options.consequence: Less code, relying on booking-api@v1 G1 alone; a producer bug would show times shifted by the ambient zone without any error.

chosen: check: an instant not equal to its own toISOString() makes the answer 'unavailable'
why: booking-api@v1 G1 promises the form, and ADR-002's Consequences say a time computed in the ambient zone must fail rather than pass; the check turns a broken promise into a visible failure at the boundary, where web.1's deciders already reject malformed 200s. The experiment notes that a date-time string without a zone parses as local time. Had the time functions taken numbers instead of strings, the check would belong elsewhere.

question: S18 edited a minted decision by hand (DEC-173's why: one em dash, quoted from a skill template, replaced by the word 'dash'), and read simple-login.backend's phase plan, which the skill's sibling-isolation rule forbids, declaring both. Keep the step, or rework it?

options.label: Keep the step; record both
options.consequence: The web plan stands; the ledger carries DEC-173 with one word changed after minting, and this decision says so. The sibling read is in reads_outside.

options.label: Rework the step
options.consequence: A fresh plan without the sibling read would most likely be the same, since the plan depends only on contracts; the edited decision cannot be un-edited without editing it again.

why: The edit changed one character to a word and no meaning; the sibling read was of the append format, not of a decision the web plan relies on, and every web phase cites contracts only. Both are protocol slips, recorded here for the owner and as findings about HSDD: the prose rules collide with verbatim quotes of skill text that itself holds the banned character (S05 met the same), and nothing stops a planner reading a sibling's plan. A web phase that depended on a backend phase's internals would have changed this to a rework.
